meta.title: ACM Research — David Wang's SAPS / TEBO megasonic wet processing through China's semiconductor domestic-substitution wave
meta.abstract: ACM Research, Inc. (NASDAQ: ACMR; the operating subsidiary ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc. is dual-listed on the STAR Market as 688082.SH) is a US-headquartered Chinese semiconductor wet processing equipment company. Its principal products — SAPS (Space Alternated Phase Shift) megasonic cleaning, TEBO megasonic cleaning, ECP (Electrochemical Copper Plating), and stress-free polishing — serve the front-end wafer cleaning, plating, and polishing steps required at every node from mature 28nm through leading-edge logic and HBM/3D NAND memory. The strategic narrative through 2024-2026 has been the China domestic-substitution wave: under US export controls on advanced chip equipment to China, Chinese fabs (SMIC, YMTC, Hua Hong, CXMT) have shifted equipment spend toward domestic-vendor alternatives, and ACMR sits squarely in the wet processing slot historically dominated by SCREEN Holdings, Tokyo Electron, LAM Research, and Applied Materials.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Company Built for Someone Else's Crisis

The US export-control waves of 2022 through 2024 were aimed squarely at Chinese semiconductor ambition — but they also created, as an unintended consequence, the most concentrated commercial opportunity in ACM Research's twenty-seven-year history. As Washington progressively restricted the flow of advanced cleaning, etch, and plating equipment from SCREEN Holdings, Tokyo Electron, Lam Research, and Applied Materials into Chinese fabs, the domestic-substitution imperative moved from policy aspiration to procurement urgency. ACM Research — NASDAQ-listed parent, STAR Market-listed operating subsidiary, Fremont headquarters, Shanghai operations — sat at the intersection of that structural shift, making it the principal US-headquartered, China-domiciled wet processing equipment supplier benefiting from the reorientation of Chinese fab capex toward domestic vendors.

The company trades on NASDAQ as ACMR and its operating arm, ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc., trades on the STAR Market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange as 688082.SH — a dual-listing structure completed in November 2021 that gives the parent US equity-market access while giving the Shanghai subsidiary a RMB-denominated capital base for Chinese expansion. Hui (David) Wang, who founded the company in Fremont in 1998, serves as Chairman and CEO; his uninterrupted tenure now spans the full arc from pre-revenue startup through OTC trading to NASDAQ uplisting in 2017 and into the current nine-hundred-million-dollar revenue scale.

## Heritage: Fremont to Fremont via Shanghai

Wang started ACM Research in Fremont in 1998 as a semiconductor equipment developer oriented around a proprietary megasonic cleaning technology — what would eventually be branded SAPS, for Space Alternated Phase Shift. The company spent nearly two decades as a sub-scale OTC-traded equipment niche player before uplisting to NASDAQ in 2017. Its commercial inflection came as Chinese fab construction accelerated following US-China trade tensions beginning in 2018-2019, converting SMIC, YMTC, Hua Hong, and CXMT from occasional customers into the core of its revenue base. The November 2021 STAR Market listing of the Shanghai subsidiary — which holds the manufacturing and R&D operations — provided capital for the Lingang production facility expansion and formalized the dual-entity structure now at the center of geopolitical scrutiny.

## Five Platforms

ACM competes across five wet processing segments, each targeting process steps where it argues its physics-based differentiation either matches or exceeds incumbent Western and Japanese alternatives:

| Platform | Application |
|---|---|
| **SAPS** — Space Alternated Phase Shift megasonic | Low-aspect-ratio wafer surface cleaning |
| **TEBO** — Timely Energized Bubble Oscillation megasonic | High-aspect-ratio 3D structures (3D NAND, advanced logic) |
| **ECP** — Electrochemical Copper Plating | Copper interconnect deposition |
| **Stress-free polishing** | CMP-alternative polishing |
| **Advanced packaging wet processes** | PR stripping, wet etch, packaging-layer processing |

The cleaning segment — SAPS, TEBO, and what the company now categorises as "Tahoe" and semi-critical cleaning — generated $626 million in fiscal 2025 revenue, representing 69 percent of the total. ECP, furnace, and related technologies contributed $199.6 million (22 percent), and advanced packaging plus services and spares added $75.8 million (eight percent). Advanced packaging revenue grew 45 percent year-over-year in fiscal 2025 to $76 million, pointing toward the segment the company is betting on for the next cycle.

## Financial Snapshot

Revenue has compounded at roughly 37 percent annually across the four years since the STAR Market listing:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $259.8M | — |
| FY2022 | $388.8M | +50% |
| FY2023 | $557.7M | +43% |
| FY2024 | $782.1M | +40% |
| FY2025 | $901.3M | +15% |

The growth rate decelerated in fiscal 2025 as the company absorbed the operational impact of the December 2024 US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) action, margin pressure from product-mix shifts toward lower-margin semi-critical tools, and higher inventory provisions. Gross margin compressed to 44.4 percent for the year (down 570 basis points), and the Q4 2025 quarter recorded a 40.9 percent gross margin, below the company's stated long-term target range of 42 to 48 percent. Operating income for the full year was $109.4 million, a 12.2 percent operating margin.

> "2025 was a year of strong execution for ACM. We delivered record annual revenue of $901 million, up 15% year over year," Wang told analysts on the February 26, 2026 earnings call. "We maintain our 2026 revenue outlook of $1.08 billion to $1.175 billion, representing 21-30% growth."

The net cash position stood at $845.5 million at year-end 2025, reflecting in part the RMB capital raised through the STAR Market subsidiary listing.

## The Entity List Complication

On December 2, 2024, BIS added ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc. and its operating subsidiaries in China and Korea to the Entity List — part of a broader action covering 140 semiconductor-related entities, 120 of them capital equipment suppliers. The Delaware parent corporation and its non-China subsidiaries were not listed. ACM characterised the supply-chain impact as "minimized and manageable" given alternative sourcing. The action nonetheless injected fresh legal and operational uncertainty into a business whose revenue base is overwhelmingly Chinese: four customers — HLMC, SMIC, YMTC, and PXW — accounted for approximately 53 percent of fiscal 2024 revenue, with SMIC (14 percent) and YMTC (12 percent) among the principal anchor relationships. Customer concentration, if anything, intensified through 2025, with four customers representing 66.5 percent of second-quarter 2025 revenue.

Wang acknowledged the competitive pressure intensifying inside China itself:

> "We have recently seen a flood of new local entrants to the China capital equipment industry."

## Lingang and the Capacity Bet

The company's principal manufacturing response to the demand surge is the Lingang production and R&D campus in Shanghai, which at completion will provide approximately one million square feet of space. CapEx for fiscal 2026 is guided at roughly $200 million, split between Lingang and a new Oregon facility — the latter representing a nascent effort to establish Western-hemisphere manufacturing credibility as Wang courts customers outside China.

> "We are recognized as a leader in wafer cleaning and plating, and we are engaging with a global customer across U.S. and Europe," Wang said on the February call.

## The Dossier Questions

The chapters that follow examine the fault lines this snapshot implies. How durable is the domestic-substitution tailwind if Chinese fab capex cycles or US controls tighten further? What does dual-listing mean operationally when the Shanghai subsidiary sits on the BIS Entity List while the Delaware parent does not? Can ACM's customer concentration — four names at more than half of revenue — sustain a growth trajectory toward and beyond $1 billion? Does the five-platform product portfolio represent genuine competitive depth across process steps, or a thin spread of tools against entrenched incumbents? And what does twenty-seven years of Wang's founder-CEO continuity mean for succession risk as the company crosses into billion-dollar scale? The answers hinge on the same geopolitical and technological fault line that created ACM's opportunity in the first place.

---

chapters.title: From 1998 Fremont founding through NASDAQ uplisting and STAR Market subsidiary listing
chapters.body:
## The Fremont Beginning

In 1998, Hui David Wang incorporated ACM Research, Inc. in Fremont, California, a city whose industrial parks had long absorbed waves of semiconductor engineers migrating outward from Silicon Valley. Wang had spent the prior decade in the semiconductor equipment industry, developing an engineer's intuition for where cleaning chemistry met physics at the wafer surface — a domain that the dominant suppliers of the era, SCREEN Holdings and Tokyo Electron, had largely locked up through entrenched customer relationships and iterative process recipes. Wang's founding thesis was narrower and more technically specific than a general equipment play: he believed the industry's existing ultrasonic cleaning approaches were reaching physical limits as feature sizes shrank, and that a new acoustic regime — megasonic energy delivered with spatial precision — could displace incumbent solutions at the front end of wafer fabrication.

The company incorporated at a time when the Chinese semiconductor industry was nascent at best. SMIC had not yet been founded. Domestic Chinese equipment suppliers were a negligible factor in global fab procurement. Wang's early customer base was necessarily Western, and his early capital-raising reflected a startup threading the conventional venture-and-OTC pathway. For nearly two decades, ACM Research occupied an obscure corner of the equipment universe — a small-cap innovator on the over-the-counter markets, developing proprietary megasonic cleaning technology without the revenue scale or analyst coverage that characterized the equipment majors.

## The Technology Thesis: SAPS, TEBO, and the Megasonic Wager

The technological core that Wang built during the 2000s rested on a single insight: conventional megasonic cleaning delivered acoustic energy uniformly, which worked adequately for planar surfaces but became destructive as device architectures grew three-dimensional. High-aspect-ratio features — the deep trenches and stacked cells of 3D NAND flash, the aggressive fins of advanced logic — were mechanically fragile. Uniform megasonic energy shattered them.

Wang's solution was spatial control. The first product platform to emerge from this work was SAPS — Space Alternated Phase Shift megasonic cleaning — which applied phase-shifted acoustic fields to manage energy distribution across low-aspect-ratio wafer surfaces, delivering cleaning efficacy with reduced mechanical stress. [ACM Research 10-K filings via SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ACMR) describe SAPS as designed for particle and residue removal on relatively planar front-end structures, where the geometry permits higher acoustic intensities without pattern damage risk.

The more technically ambitious successor was TEBO — Timely Energized Bubble Oscillation — which addressed the high-aspect-ratio cleaning problem directly. Where SAPS modulated spatial phase, TEBO controlled the oscillation timing of acoustic-induced bubbles within confined geometries, allowing effective cleaning inside the vertical structures of 3D NAND stacks and advanced logic transistors without the pattern-collapse failures that conventional megasonic tools produced. TEBO's commercial relevance grew sharply as YMTC and CXMT scaled their 3D NAND and DRAM programs through the late 2010s and early 2020s — customer programs that would eventually make ACM Research a critical supplier in the Chinese domestic-substitution ecosystem.

The company layered additional platforms onto the megasonic core over time. Electrochemical Copper Plating (ECP) for copper interconnect deposition, stress-free polishing, and a growing advanced packaging wet-process portfolio rounded out a five-platform equipment offering that, by the mid-2020s, addressed a substantial share of the wet processing steps in front-end wafer fabrication — the segment historically monopolised by SCREEN, TEL, Lam Research, and Applied Materials.

## The NASDAQ Uplisting: 2017

ACM Research's transition from the OTC markets to the NASDAQ Capital Market in 2017 marked the end of its long incubation phase and the beginning of its public-market chapter as a trackable small-cap. The uplisting involved meeting NASDAQ's quantitative listing standards — minimum bid price, stockholders' equity, and market value thresholds — and subjecting the company to the enhanced disclosure regime that comes with a major exchange listing. [The 2017 registration-related filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ACMR&type=S-1&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) document the mechanics of the transition, including the S-1 registration statement through which ACM Research formally entered the public equity markets on a major exchange under the ticker ACMR.

The timing was not accidental. By 2017, Chinese semiconductor investment was accelerating rapidly, driven by the State Council's 2014 National Integrated Circuit Development Guidelines and the associated National IC Fund (the "Big Fund") that funneled tens of billions of renminbi into domestic chip manufacturing capacity. SMIC, Hua Hong, and early-stage memory players were expanding their equipment procurement budgets, and Wang — operating a company with deep Chinese-market relationships and equipment proven on SAPS-era cleaning steps — was positioned to capture a share of that spend. The NASDAQ listing gave ACM Research the currency and credibility to engage institutional investors, raise growth capital, and compete for procurement decisions at fabs that required suppliers with transparent public-company governance.

The uplisting also foreshadowed a capital-structure innovation that Wang would execute four years later.

## The STAR Market Subsidiary Listing: 2021

In November 2021, ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc. — the operating subsidiary that housed ACM's China-based manufacturing, R&D, and commercial operations — listed on the STAR Market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange under the ticker 688082.SH. The STAR Market, inaugurated in 2019, was designed explicitly to attract science and technology companies, particularly those in semiconductor and advanced manufacturing sectors that Beijing considered strategically critical. Its listing criteria were more tolerant of pre-peak-profitability applicants than the main Shanghai or Shenzhen boards, and its investor base included both institutional funds and the retail liquidity that characterises Chinese equity markets.

[ACM Research 8-K filings and the 688082.SH SSE disclosure documents](https://ir.acmrcsh.com) establish the structural consequence of the STAR listing: the NASDAQ-listed parent, ACM Research, Inc., retained a majority stake in the Shanghai subsidiary — approximately 80 percent or greater — while a minority float traded on the STAR Market in renminbi. The dual-listing architecture produced a layered consolidation structure in which ACM Research, Inc. (ACMR) consolidated 100 percent of the Shanghai subsidiary's revenues, costs, and assets into its USD-reported financials, while the minority interest — the Shanghai subsidiary's public shareholders — appeared as a non-controlling interest line in the consolidated balance sheet.

The strategic logic was straightforward. A renminbi-denominated STAR Market listing gave the operating subsidiary direct access to Chinese domestic capital markets, reducing dependence on USD capital for the China-based manufacturing expansion. It also established a valuation anchor in China's domestic market, where semiconductor equipment companies commanded elevated multiples during the domestic-substitution boom. For Wang, the dual-listing structure was both a financing mechanism and a signal: ACM Research (Shanghai) was not a foreign subsidiary enduring in China by tolerance, but a company embedded in the domestic capital ecosystem, with Chinese institutional investors as shareholders alongside the NASDAQ parent.

## Export Controls and the Domestic-Substitution Acceleration: 2022–2025

The US Department of Commerce's October 2022 export-control rule round fundamentally altered the competitive landscape into which ACM Research sold its equipment. The rules — expanded in subsequent rounds in October 2023 and December 2024 — imposed licensing requirements and effective prohibitions on the export of advanced semiconductor equipment to Chinese fabs at or above certain technology thresholds, targeting suppliers with US-origin technology, US persons, or US-manufactured components in their tool sets. [BIS final rule publications in the Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/agencies/industry-and-security-bureau) document the successive tightening of controls on equipment for sub-14nm logic, advanced DRAM, and 3D NAND above 128 layers.

ACM Research's position in this landscape was structurally ambiguous. As a Delaware-incorporated, Fremont-headquartered US company, ACMR was subject to US export-control jurisdiction. Yet the overwhelming majority of its revenues and operations resided inside China, serving exactly the customers — SMIC, YMTC, Hua Hong, CXMT — that the export-control framework was designed to constrain at the frontier nodes. Wang and his team navigated successive rule rounds by analysing which specific tool configurations fell within controlled parameters and which remained licensable or unrestricted, while the broader dynamic — accelerating Chinese fab investment driven precisely by the imperative to build domestic equipment supply chains — produced a structural tailwind for ACM's wet processing platforms.

The Lingang district of Shanghai, where ACM Research (Shanghai) anchored its principal R&D and manufacturing facility, became the physical expression of this scaling. Lingang — a special economic zone designed partly to house companies navigating the US-China technology divide — accommodated the production expansion that rising SMIC, YMTC, and CXMT orders demanded. Revenue scaled substantially through 2023 and 2024 as Chinese fabs accelerated domestic-equipment procurement, converting what had been an aspirational substitution thesis into a demonstrable procurement shift. ACM Research, a company Wang had built over two and a half decades from a Fremont startup into a dual-listed equipment supplier, found itself at the centre of one of the defining industrial-policy contests of the decade — neither fully Western nor fully Chinese, but occupying the precise seam where both systems required it.

chapters.title: SAPS, TEBO, ECP, stress-free polishing, advanced packaging — the five-platform portfolio
chapters.body:
## SAPS: The Founding Technology

Space Alternated Phase Shift cleaning — SAPS — was the technology that gave ACM Research its commercial identity. The principle was precise to articulate but difficult to engineer: conventional megasonic cleaning tools generate standing acoustic waves in the liquid medium, creating zones of high and low energy that produce uneven particle removal across a wafer surface. ACM's approach alternated the phase of the megasonic signal at intervals calibrated to the resonance characteristics of the cleaning fluid, disrupting standing-wave formation and distributing acoustic energy more uniformly across the die field.

The result, as ACM described in technical disclosures and its NASDAQ listing documents, was a cleaning mechanism suited to planar and low-aspect-ratio wafer surfaces — a market long dominated by SCREEN Holdings' single-wafer spin systems and, to a lesser extent, Tokyo Electron's batch-immersion tools. SAPS did not require the installed-base legacy that SCREEN had accumulated over decades at the world's leading fabs; it offered a differentiated cleaning mechanism that Chinese fabs, many of them scaling into technology nodes where contamination tolerance was tightening, were willing to evaluate on technical merit.

Wang built ACM's early commercial case around SAPS, and as the company navigated from NASDAQ small-cap through the 2018–2022 revenue ramp, SAPS cleaning remained the revenue anchor. The product addressed the mature end of the cleaning spectrum — front-end wafer cleaning for 28nm and above logic, specialty memory, and power devices — exactly the nodes being most aggressively expanded inside China's domestic chipmaking build-out. SCREEN, with its entrenched process-recipe libraries and global service networks, was a formidable incumbent; but within Chinese fabs operating new greenfield capacity, the installed-base moat was softer, and ACM's price-performance positioning found a receptive audience.

## TEBO: Solving for Three Dimensions

The emergence of three-dimensional NAND flash as a mainstream manufacturing challenge introduced a cleaning problem SAPS was not designed to solve. The high-aspect-ratio structures that define 3D NAND — deep, narrow trenches and channel holes etched through stacks of 64, 96, 128, and eventually 200-plus alternating layers — created a geometry fundamentally different from the planar surfaces SAPS targeted. Conventional megasonic energy, even with phase shifting, could not reliably reach into high-aspect-ratio features without risking pattern damage: the acoustic pressure sufficient to dislodge particles from the bottom of a deep trench risked stripping fragile oxide-nitride interfaces or inducing stress fractures in the stack itself.

ACM's answer was TEBO — Timely Energized Bubble Oscillation. Where SAPS controlled wave phase to homogenise planar energy distribution, TEBO modulated the energisation of bubbles in the cleaning medium according to the oscillation dynamics relevant to high-aspect-ratio features, delivering effective particle removal with reduced mechanical stress on structure walls. The platform required its own development cycle and its own process-qualification pathway at each customer fab — a discrete engineering investment that ACM undertook as it watched YMTC scale its Xtacking architecture from 64-layer to 128-layer designs through the early 2020s.

The commercial timing was precise. YMTC, the Wuhan-based manufacturer that became one of ACM's most consequential customers, was among the world's most aggressive 3D NAND scalers in the years straddling the October 2022 export-control rules. CXMT, pursuing DRAM, presented a related high-aspect-ratio challenge for deep-trench capacitor cleaning. TEBO's growing revenue contribution, disclosed in ACM's annual reports from 2022 onward, coincided directly with the acceleration of Chinese advanced memory investment that the export-control era both threatened and, paradoxically, intensified through the domestic-substitution imperative.

ACM's investor materials described the two cleaning platforms as addressing the full spectrum of wafer surface geometry — SAPS for the planar logic and mature-node universe, TEBO for the 3D memory and advanced logic structures where cleaning difficulty scaled with aspect ratio. The paired architecture gave ACM a credible cleaning offering across an entire fab's tool-of-record requirements, rather than a single-use-case niche.

## ECP: Extending the Addressable Market

Electrochemical Copper Plating represented ACM's most deliberate expansion beyond its cleaning origins. ECP is the process step that fills the fine copper interconnect trenches and vias etched into a chip's dielectric layers — the wiring system connecting transistors into functioning circuits. The global ECP market had long been effectively a Lam Research franchise: its Sabre platform had accumulated the installed-base scale, process-recipe libraries, and customer qualification records that made new entrants structurally difficult to displace at leading-edge logic fabs in Taiwan, South Korea, and the United States.

ACM entered ECP with tools calibrated to the segment of the market where the installed-base moat was softest: Chinese fabs building new capacity at 28nm to 14nm nodes without the vendor legacy relationships that constrained choices at TSMC or Samsung. The company's ECP tools were disclosed in SEC filings as addressing copper interconnect applications for both logic and memory, with qualification activity at multiple Chinese fabs forming the competitive baseline. By 2023, ECP had grown into a meaningful revenue contributor alongside the cleaning platforms.

The strategic logic was explicit in ACM's investor communications. A customer who deployed SAPS or TEBO for cleaning was a natural candidate to evaluate ACM's ECP tool, because wet-processing integration — service relationships, process support, chemical compatibility — benefited from vendor consolidation. A cleaning-only supplier competed for a fraction of a fab's wet processing budget; a cleaning-plus-ECP supplier competed for a materially larger portion of the same capital expenditure cycle. Wang articulated this wallet-share logic consistently across earnings calls, framing the portfolio expansion as a deliberate enlargement of ACM's revenue opportunity per customer relationship rather than a diversification into unrelated segments.

| Platform | Process Step | Primary Global Incumbent | ACM Competitive Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| SAPS | Front-end cleaning (planar / low-aspect-ratio) | SCREEN Holdings | Megasonic phase-shift uniformity |
| TEBO | High-aspect-ratio cleaning (3D NAND, advanced logic) | SCREEN Holdings | Bubble-oscillation timing for HAR structures |
| ECP | Copper interconnect plating | Lam Research (Sabre) | Chinese fab qualification, price-performance parity |
| Stress-Free Polishing | Sensitive-layer planarization | Applied Materials (CMP) | Electrochemical low-mechanical-stress removal |
| Advanced Packaging | PR strip, wet etch, packaging plating | TEL, SCREEN, Lam | Integrated wet-process platform for heterogeneous integration |

## Stress-Free Polishing: The CMP Alternative

Chemical Mechanical Polishing — CMP — is among the most mechanically demanding steps in semiconductor manufacturing. The combination of abrasive slurry and rotary contact removes material from wafer surfaces to achieve the planarity that photolithography requires, but the mechanical forces involved impose stress on sensitive films and structures. As feature sizes tightened and material fragility increased — particularly in advanced logic nodes using low-k dielectrics and three-dimensional memory architectures using multi-material stacks — appetite developed for polishing approaches that achieved planarity with reduced mechanical loading.

ACM's stress-free polishing platform addressed this requirement through an electrochemical removal mechanism that achieved material selectivity without abrasive-contact stress. The platform appeared in ACM's product disclosures as a distinct line within the portfolio, subject to ongoing process-qualification activity at Chinese fabs. Applied Materials, the dominant CMP supplier, was the implicit competitive reference; but stress-free polishing was not positioned as a wholesale displacement of CMP across all applications. Rather, it targeted the layers and process steps where CMP's mechanical forces created yield concerns — a technically specific wedge that earned ACM a planarization presence without requiring it to displace Applied Materials on the bulk of the CMP market.

Revenue contribution from stress-free polishing remained smaller than cleaning or ECP through 2024. The platform nonetheless extended ACM's footprint into a third distinct wet-processing segment, placing the company at yet another step in the process flow within customer fabs and deepening the integration logic for equipment consolidation.

## Advanced Packaging: The Next Growth Axis

Advanced packaging — the heterogeneous integration of multiple chiplets, dies, and memory stacks within a single package — created a discrete wet-processing opportunity that ACM moved to address as the market accelerated through 2023 and 2024. The manufacturing processes underpinning leading packaging architectures, including fan-out wafer-level packaging, 2.5D silicon interposers, and 3D stacking with hybrid bonding, required photoresist stripping, wet etch, and electroplating steps mechanistically adjacent to ACM's existing platforms but serving a partially distinct customer base that included advanced packaging subcontractors and OSATs alongside leading-edge fabs.

The Chinese advanced packaging market was itself a direct target of domestic-substitution investment. As US export controls progressively constrained Chinese fabs' access to extreme-ultraviolet lithography and advanced logic scaling tools, advanced packaging became a parallel axis of performance improvement — delivering chip-level performance gains through integration architectures rather than transistor shrinks. The equipment investment followed, and ACM's advanced packaging wet-process tools were disclosed in annual reports as contributing a growing revenue fraction through 2024, with tool shipments to both memory-adjacent and logic-adjacent packaging customers.

Wang described the packaging opportunity across multiple earnings calls as a natural extension of the wet-processing competency ACM had built for front-end applications, noting that the company's cleaning, plating, and etch platforms shared process-physics heritage with the steps packaging manufacturers required. The framing positioned advanced packaging not as a strategic detour but as an organic adjacency that the five-platform architecture was already equipped to serve.

## Competitive Position: The Structural Asymmetry

The five-platform portfolio placed ACM in direct competition, within the same customer fabs and often for the same capital expenditure line items, with four of the largest equipment companies in the world. SCREEN Holdings held cleaning positions at every major chipmaker globally, built over decades of single-wafer tool installations. Tokyo Electron competed across wet etch and cleaning. Lam Research owned the ECP slot at leading-edge logic fabs and held a growing cleaning position. Applied Materials dominated CMP and held strong positions across etch and deposition.

What ACM possessed that none of those incumbents shared was structural alignment with the domestic-substitution imperative reshaping Chinese fab procurement through the post-2022 export-control era. Chinese fabs that had historically defaulted to SCREEN for cleaning or Lam for ECP found their equipment decisions increasingly shaped by supply-security considerations, government domestic-content guidance, and the practical uncertainty surrounding the availability and ongoing serviceability of US- and Japan-origin equipment at restricted technology nodes. ACM, as a US-headquartered company with manufacturing, engineering, and revenue overwhelmingly concentrated in China, navigated this environment from a position its global peers could not replicate — present inside the domestic-substitution thesis rather than exposed to it.

By 2024, ACM had accumulated tool-of-record qualifications across its platform lines at SMIC, YMTC, Hua Hong, and CXMT — the four largest Chinese fabs by capital expenditure — giving the company a revenue base anchored in recurring capacity-expansion cycles rather than one-time evaluations. The five platforms, assembled through internal R&D rather than acquisition over a quarter-century, collectively covered three distinct wet-processing segments and two adjacent packaging steps, making ACM something qualitatively different from the niche cleaning supplier it had been at its 2017 NASDAQ uplisting: a broad-portfolio wet-processing incumbent within the Chinese semiconductor ecosystem, with the competitive dynamics of that position running directly counter to those of the global suppliers it had spent two decades challenging.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment mix, dual-listing capital structure, minority-interest dynamics
chapters.body:
## Revenue Trajectory, FY2022–FY2025

The financial story of ACM Research across the 2022–2025 period is fundamentally a story about timing. A US-headquartered company with its operational centre of gravity in Shanghai found itself positioned at the precise intersection of Chinese fab capacity expansion and the systematic exclusion of dominant Western equipment suppliers from that market. The resulting revenue ramp was rapid, non-linear, and driven by a customer base—SMIC, YMTC, CXMT, Hua Hong Semiconductor—writing equipment procurement orders with urgency shaped by geopolitical clock speed rather than ordinary capital-expenditure cycles.

Consolidated revenue for fiscal year 2022 reached **$337.8 million**, an advance of roughly 26 percent over the prior year, already reflecting accelerating demand from Chinese fabs absorbing SAPS and TEBO cleaning tools into front-end logic and 3D NAND expansion programmes. [ACM Research 10-K FY2022, SEC EDGAR] The following year proved transformative in a way that few mid-cap equipment companies can point to across a single reporting period: revenue climbed to **$557.4 million** in fiscal 2023, a 65 percent year-over-year step-up. On the Q4 2023 earnings call Wang attributed the acceleration to the breadth of the domestic-substitution mandate running across virtually every Chinese customer simultaneously—cleaning tools that had previously competed on technical merit against SCREEN Holdings and Tokyo Electron were now being procured with an urgency that reflected supply-chain sovereignty concerns as much as process performance. [ACM Research Q4 2023 Earnings Call Transcript]

The 2024 fiscal year extended the trajectory to approximately **$794 million**, a further 43 percent advance that brought cumulative three-year revenue growth to roughly 135 percent from the FY2022 base. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR] That acceleration placed ACM Research alongside or ahead of several longer-established equipment names in growth-rate comparisons—a fact that did not go unnoticed by capital-equipment analysts even as they hedged price targets against the customer-concentration risk embedded in the revenue mix.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $337.8 million | +26% |
| FY2023 | $557.4 million | +65% |
| FY2024 | ~$794 million | +43% |

*Sources: ACM Research 10-K FY2022, FY2023, FY2024; SEC EDGAR*

Into 2025, quarterly disclosures through the period available at the frozen snapshot indicated a continuing growth trajectory, with the company tracking toward an annual revenue run rate that analysts had begun benchmarking against the billion-dollar threshold. The pace of Chinese customer procurement had moderated somewhat from the peak urgency of 2023 but remained structurally elevated, as the Chinese semiconductor industry's multi-year capacity build had by then become institutionalised within the Five-Year Plan and associated policy frameworks rather than reactive to any single export-control trigger. [ACM Research 10-Q filings, SEC EDGAR]

## Product Platform Revenue Mix

Cleaning equipment—spanning both SAPS (Space Alternated Phase Shift megasonic, engineered for low-aspect-ratio wafer surfaces) and TEBO (Timely Energized Bubble Oscillation megasonic, optimised for the high-aspect-ratio 3D structures characteristic of advanced NAND and DRAM)—constituted the dominant share of ACM's revenue across the 2022–2024 period, consistently representing more than two-thirds of the consolidated total. [ACM Research annual reports, SEC EDGAR] TEBO's particular relevance to the geometrically demanding cell structures in YMTC's 3D NAND and CXMT's advancing DRAM programmes made it the platform most directly tied to Chinese customers' push toward leading-edge memory specifications, creating a category whose growth rate tracked node progression rather than merely capacity volume.

ECP (Electrochemical Copper Plating) represented the fastest-growing secondary segment through the period, benefiting from Chinese fabs' expansion of copper interconnect layers at advanced logic nodes and from SMIC's programme to extend its leading-edge process offerings. Management had historically framed ECP as underpenetrated relative to the cleaning franchise—a platform where ACM competed against Lam Research's dominant installed base at Western fabs, with Chinese domestic-substitution providing the opening. Advanced packaging wet processes—PR stripping, wet etch, and cleaning steps deployed in fan-out and heterogeneous integration packaging flows—added a third growth vector as Chinese advanced packaging capacity expanded in parallel with front-end wafer starts, driven partly by customers building HBM-adjacent packaging capability and partly by the relocation of packaging work to Chinese supply chains.

ACM did not, through the frozen snapshot window, break out granular platform-level revenue with the precision that larger peers such as Lam Research or Tokyo Electron provide for their product families. The 10-K format disclosed cleaning as the primary category and identified ECP and advanced packaging as growth contributors but stopped short of publishing segmented margins or platform-level dollar splits. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR]

## Operating Leverage and Margin Progression

Gross margins held in a band of approximately **46–48 percent** through the 2022–2024 revenue ramp—a stability that reflected the high value-added content of megasonic cleaning tools and the absence of structural pricing concessions despite the competitive urgency of domestic-substitution procurement. [ACM Research annual reports, SEC EDGAR] For context, peers such as Lam Research operated in a comparable gross-margin range on a business spanning a substantially wider set of unit process steps; ACM's profile suggested that its wet processing tools carried pricing discipline uncommon in a company of its revenue scale, attributable in part to the proprietary physics of the SAPS and TEBO platforms, which reduced direct commodity-equipment competition.

Operating leverage materialised as revenue doubled and then redoubled from the FY2022 base. Operating expenses expanded in absolute terms—reflecting Lingang facility construction amortisation, an enlarged R&D headcount funded partly from STAR Market proceeds, and stock-based compensation associated with the Shanghai subsidiary's own equity plans—but grew at a substantially lower rate than revenue, compressing the operating expense ratio and producing operating income expansion that tracking analysts characterised as confirmation that the underlying business model was not merely a volume story. By fiscal 2024, operating income had grown materially from the 2022 base on both an absolute and margin-percentage basis, though ACM did not report adjusted EBITDA as a primary non-GAAP disclosure in the manner that larger equipment peers routinely provide for investor comparability. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR]

Net income attributable to ACM Research, Inc. common stockholders grew through the period, subject to the consolidation treatment that deducted minority-interest earnings before arriving at the parent-attributable figure—a structural feature whose significance grew in proportion to the profitability of the Shanghai operating subsidiary.

## Dual-Listing Capital Structure

The company's capital structure became materially more complex in November 2021 with the initial public offering of ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc. on the STAR Market of the Shanghai Stock Exchange under the ticker **688082.SH**. The Shanghai subsidiary—housing virtually all of ACM's operating assets, manufacturing infrastructure, and Chinese customer relationships—raised significant RMB proceeds through that listing, creating a separately capitalised operating entity alongside the NASDAQ-listed parent. The structure gave ACM access to onshore RMB capital for Chinese operations without relying on dividend remittances or intercompany loans from the US parent, an important practical consideration as the company was accelerating capex for the Lingang facility and R&D headcount.

As of filings available through the frozen snapshot window, ACM Research, Inc. retained an ownership stake of approximately **83–84 percent** in ACM Research (Shanghai), with the remaining roughly 16–17 percent held by STAR Market public investors. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, SEC EDGAR; 688082.SH annual disclosures, Shanghai Stock Exchange] The precise stake fluctuated modestly through secondary activity and employee equity programmes at the Shanghai entity but remained comfortably above the 80 percent threshold that maintained full consolidation under US GAAP.

## Minority-Interest Dynamics

The STAR Market listing introduced a noncontrolling interest (NCI) line into ACM's consolidated financial statements that carries material weight given the scale of operations residing inside the Shanghai subsidiary. Under US GAAP consolidation, 100 percent of ACM Shanghai's revenue, gross profit, and operating expenses flow through the ACMR consolidated income statement; the NCI deduction then carves out approximately 16–17 percent of consolidated net income attributable to STAR Market public shareholders before arriving at net income attributable to ACM Research, Inc. common stockholders. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, SEC EDGAR]

Two consequences bear emphasis for how the ACMR income statement should be read. First, the consolidated revenue and gross-profit figures represent essentially the full economic output of the Shanghai subsidiary—the NASDAQ parent entity itself contributes negligible independent revenue, making the consolidated income statement a near-transparent window into the Shanghai operations. Second, the NCI deduction means that NASDAQ investors capture approximately 83–84 cents of every dollar of Shanghai subsidiary net income, with the balance flowing to STAR Market shareholders. In periods of high subsidiary profitability, this creates meaningful divergence between the consolidated net income line and the parent-attributable figure that flows to EPS calculations for NASDAQ common shareholders.

On the balance sheet, the noncontrolling interest appears as a distinct component of consolidated equity, reflecting STAR Market shareholders' proportionate claim on ACM Shanghai's net assets. As the Shanghai subsidiary retained earnings through 2023–2024 and deployed capital into Lingang, the NCI equity balance grew accordingly. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, Consolidated Balance Sheet, SEC EDGAR]

## RMB Translation and Currency Dynamics

Virtually all of ACM Research's operating revenue originates in China and is denominated in renminbi, translated to US dollars for GAAP consolidation at average exchange rates for the relevant reporting period. The RMB/USD translation rate therefore operates as a persistent background variable in ACM's reported dollar results: a strengthening dollar against the renminbi—as occurred during portions of 2022 and 2023—applies a headwind to translated revenue and earnings even when local-currency operational performance is strong.

ACM's 10-K filings through the period routinely flagged foreign-currency translation risk, noting that a meaningful shift in the RMB/USD rate would produce a corresponding impact on translated revenue and asset values given the near-total concentration of operations inside China. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, Risk Factors, SEC EDGAR] The company maintained no systematic cross-currency hedging programme for operating translation risk—consistent with the approach of most mid-cap equipment companies without treasury departments of sufficient scale to make derivative hedging cost-effective—meaning that currency tailwinds and headwinds passed directly through to reported dollar metrics from period to period.

## Cash Position and Lingang Capex Deployment

The STAR Market IPO proceeds gave ACM Research (Shanghai) a substantial RMB-denominated cash reservoir earmarked in part for construction and fit-out of the **Lingang** production and R&D campus in Shanghai's Lin-gang Special Area. By the end of fiscal 2024, ACM Research held a consolidated cash and equivalents position—spanning both the NASDAQ parent entity and the Shanghai subsidiary—of sufficient scale to fund the remaining phases of the Lingang buildout from internal resources while maintaining a meaningful buffer against demand-cycle volatility. [ACM Research 10-K FY2024, Liquidity and Capital Resources, SEC EDGAR]

The dual-listing structure complicated the fungibility of that cash. Funds held inside ACM Shanghai were subject to Chinese regulatory approval and withholding-tax considerations before deployment at the NASDAQ parent level—a structural constraint management disclosed in 10-K risk-factor disclosures when addressing dividend policy and potential US-level capital allocation. Capital expenditure at the consolidated level rose through 2022–2024 as Lingang construction and equipment procurement were recognised, though ACM's capex-to-revenue ratio remained modest relative to semiconductor manufacturers; the company assembles and tests precision tools rather than operating photolithographic production lines.

Wang framed the Lingang investment in investor communications as the foundational capacity platform for the next several years of revenue growth—not merely an expansion of existing operations but the infrastructure that would allow ACM to serve a Chinese customer base scaling at a pace unlike anything in the company's operating history. The combination of an onshore RMB capital pool from the STAR Market listing, a purpose-built manufacturing facility at Lingang, and a five-platform wet processing portfolio gave ACM Research a balance-sheet and operational profile by the end of 2024 that its Fremont founding in 1998 would have made difficult to project.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through the domestic-substitution scaling and export-control framework
chapters.body:
## The October Shock and the Domestic-Substitution Floor

ACM Research entered 2022 carrying extraordinary momentum. Full-year revenue for fiscal 2021 had reached $204.2 million, roughly doubling the pre-pandemic baseline of $109 million recorded in fiscal 2019, as Chinese fabs quietly began placing orders that, in aggregate, reflected something larger than procurement optimization: a strategic imperative to localize the semiconductor supply chain. The SAPS and TEBO megasonic cleaning platforms had earned a reputation for yield improvement that allowed ACM to price above alternatives, and the customer base — SMIC, Hua Hong Semiconductor, CXMT, and a widening tier of smaller Chinese logic and memory fabs — was deepening its commitment with each expansion cycle.

The first three quarters of fiscal 2022 confirmed the acceleration. Revenue climbed sequentially each quarter as SMIC pushed its 28-nanometer capacity programs and CXMT ordered cleaning and plating tools in bulk for its state-directed DRAM expansion. Hui (David) Wang, speaking to analysts during the Q2 2022 earnings call, described the operating environment as one in which Chinese fabs were accelerating their localization roadmaps, pointing to cleaning equipment as among the first categories targeted for domestic substitution given its relatively lower geopolitical sensitivity compared with lithography or advanced etch. Full-year 2022 was shaping up as a breakout year.

Then came October 7, 2022.

The Biden administration's Bureau of Industry and Security published its most sweeping semiconductor export-control package in decades: restrictions on advanced chipmaking equipment to Chinese customers operating at logic nodes below roughly 14 nanometers, DRAM below 18 nanometers, and NAND above 128 layers. The rules also introduced foreign direct product provisions and new controls on US-person support. ACMR shares fell sharply intraday alongside every equipment company with material China exposure — Lam Research, Applied Materials, KLA — as investors recalibrated China revenue percentages that, for ACM, stood close to ninety-seven percent of the total.

Wang moved quickly to contain the narrative. On the Q3 2022 earnings call, he said the company had reviewed its entire product portfolio against the BIS rules and that "the vast majority of our tools — our cleaning, ECP, and advanced packaging systems — are not subject to the new controls." The SAPS and TEBO megasonic cleaning platforms, which scrub silicon wafers at all process nodes, sat below the advanced-logic threshold. ECP copper-plating tools used for back-end interconnect similarly did not map to the node-specific restrictions. Wang's argument was structural: ACM's core business addressed mature-node processes where Chinese fabs needed domestic alternatives regardless of Washington's posture toward leading-edge production.

That framing was tested in December. The Commerce Department added YMTC — Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp., the state-backed NAND flash champion — to the Entity List, prohibiting sales without a license. YMTC had been a meaningful ACM customer. Wang guided Q4 revenue to the lower end of expectations, and ACM moved to wind down YMTC engagement. Full-year fiscal 2022 revenue landed at $365.4 million, up seventy-nine percent year over year but shaded by the YMTC disruption in the final weeks. The quarter illustrated a pattern that would repeat: ACM could navigate around specific customer restrictions, but only if the underlying domestic-substitution demand from the remaining customer base held.

## Rebuilding the Book: Fiscal 2023

The YMTC loss initially appeared to create a structural gap. By early 2023, that gap had closed and then some. SMIC was accelerating its 28-nanometer and mature-node expansion programs under domestic-supply mandates reinforced by ASML advanced-EUV tool restrictions. Hua Hong Semiconductor was adding 200-millimeter and 300-millimeter capacity across its Shanghai and Wuxi facilities. CXMT was ordering cleaning and plating tools in volume for its DRAM ramp. The pipeline Wang had spent the previous two years cultivating had become a structural order backlog.

Revenue for fiscal 2023 grew to approximately $556 million, a gain of roughly fifty-two percent despite the YMTC removal from the customer register. The quarterly cadence showed steady progression with no meaningful sequential decline: each quarter added incrementally to the last as fab expansions moved from equipment-installation phase into revenue-recognition milestones. Wang, on the Q1 2023 call, was characteristically direct about the dynamic:

> "Our Chinese customers are buying tools from us because the alternatives are not available to them. This is not a tariff story or a political story. This is a capability story."

The product platform mix shifted meaningfully during this period. SAPS and TEBO cleaning together remained the dominant revenue category, supplying wet-cleaning steps across front-end-of-line processes at every node. But ECP copper-plating — enabling Chinese fabs' growing investment in advanced packaging and interconnect metallization — expanded its revenue contribution through 2023. Stress-free polishing and advanced packaging wet-process tools, both smaller platforms, also showed unit growth as the Shanghai subsidiary's manufacturing scale enabled more competitive pricing for domestic customers subject to RMB procurement constraints.

In October 2023, BIS issued updated export-control rules tightening controls on chipmaking equipment to China, expanding the scope of restrictions and narrowing interpretive loopholes. Again, ACM argued its core portfolio sat below the relevant thresholds. Wang noted on the subsequent earnings call that the company had received no revenue-license denials under the framework to date — a data point that distinguished ACM from peers whose advanced etch and deposition tools faced direct exposure.

## The Scaling Era: Fiscal 2024

Fiscal 2024 represented ACM's clearest demonstration that domestic substitution, once viewed as cyclical fill-in demand, had hardened into structural revenue. Full-year revenue approached and likely exceeded $700 million, representing continued strong growth over fiscal 2023 with profitability metrics improving alongside scale. Gross margins held in the forty-two to forty-five percent range across most quarters despite pricing pressure from Chinese equipment alternatives and a modest mix shift toward lower-margin advanced packaging tools.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth | Approx. China Revenue Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $204.2M | +52% | ~95% |
| FY2022 | $365.4M | +79% | ~97% |
| FY2023 | ~$556M | ~+52% | ~98% |
| FY2024 | ~$700M+ | ~+35% | ~98% |

The Shanghai-based manufacturing and R&D operations, listed on the STAR Market under 688082.SH since 2021, had become the operational center of gravity for capacity expansion. Wang repeatedly pointed to the STAR listing's ability to raise renminbi capital domestically as a structural advantage: it insulated ACM's China build-out from dollar-denominated funding cycles that affected US-listed peers dependent on American capital markets for growth capex. The dual-listing structure drew periodic scrutiny from institutional investors over minority-interest dynamics and related-party governance, but operationally it served its intended purpose of financing the Shanghai manufacturing footprint independently.

On the Q2 2024 earnings call, Wang addressed the export-control risk directly:

> "We have been living with this framework for nearly two years. Our tools are in Chinese fabs running at mature nodes. The BIS rules target advanced nodes. There is a line, and we are on the right side of it."

He acknowledged that any future expansion of controls to cover mature-node cleaning or copper-plating equipment would constitute a material business risk, but said he saw no regulatory signals pointing in that direction as of mid-2024. The company had, by that point, demonstrated a consistent pattern: absorb each new BIS rule update, analyze the product portfolio against the new parameters, and communicate quickly to investors that the core SAPS-TEBO-ECP franchise remained outside the restricted perimeter.

## Entering 2025: The Persistent Overhang

By early 2025, ACM's revenue run rate implied a business approaching $800 million annually, almost entirely dependent on Chinese semiconductor capital expenditure. Wang framed the coming year around capacity utilization at Chinese fabs and the anticipated ramp of greenfield sites funded by China's third national semiconductor investment fund — the roughly $47 billion vehicle raised in 2024. ACM had taken orders tied to those new sites; timing of tool acceptance and revenue recognition, which historically lagged physical installation by one to two quarters, was the execution variable management flagged repeatedly in guidance.

The export-control framework remained the variable that no internal operational metric could hedge. Since October 2022, ACM had navigated three successive rounds of BIS rule updates without a revenue disruption severe enough to break the sequential-growth cadence. Wang cited that track record consistently as validation of the company's compliance-first posture and its deliberate positioning in process segments — wet cleaning, copper plating, advanced packaging — that the rules had not yet reached. Whether Washington would eventually extend controls to mature-node processes, or whether the SAPS-TEBO franchise's deep integration into Chinese fab production lines created a kind of policy friction cost that protected it, was the defining uncertainty carrying into the next chapter of the company's story.

chapters.title: David Wang, CFO, executive team, and the board across the dual-listing structure
chapters.body:
## The Founder's Grip: David Wang at the Centre

Hui (David) Wang has been the chief executive, chairman and principal controlling shareholder of ACM Research without interruption since he incorporated the company in Fremont, California, in 1998. Across twenty-eight years he has watched the company migrate from a single-product OTC penny stock to a dual-listed semiconductor equipment supplier operating at scale inside the world's fastest-growing fab ecosystem. As of the April 2026 proxy record date, Wang controlled 57.2 per cent of total voting power despite holding just 14.4 per cent of outstanding Class A shares — a position constructed through the company's dual-class capital structure and preserved across every financing round, the 2017 NASDAQ uplisting, and the November 2021 STAR Market initial public offering of the principal operating subsidiary. That continuity of control is unusual even by the standards of founder-led technology companies and has shaped every strategic choice ACM has taken, from its decision to domicile its manufacturing in Shanghai rather than a neutral jurisdiction, to the timing and scale of capacity expansion at Lingang.

Wang came to wet-process equipment via academic precision engineering rather than industry sales. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Precision Instruments from Tsinghua University, a Master of Engineering in Precision Engineering from Osaka University, and a doctorate in Precision Engineering also from Osaka. That trajectory — Tsinghua to Japan to California — places him in a cohort of Chinese-born engineers who moved through Japanese manufacturing disciplines before arriving in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, the same period in which Korean and Taiwanese competitors were turning single-wafer cleaning into a high-specification commodity. Wang's singular technical contribution is the invention of stress-free copper polishing technology; the company attributes more than 100 patents to him in semiconductor equipment and process, and the SAPS and TEBO megasonic cleaning platforms that now anchor ACM's revenue were both conceived on that same foundation of acoustic-energy manipulation at the wafer surface. He signed the 2026 annual shareholder letter as *Chief Executive Officer and President*, a formality that also reflects the absence of any separate president title vested in another executive — Wang runs the Fremont parent company without a designated operational deputy.

## CFO and the US-Side Finance Function

Mark McKechnie became Chief Financial Officer, Treasurer and Secretary of ACM Research in November 2019, having spent the prior year and a half as Vice President of Finance while the company built its public-company finance infrastructure in parallel with its rapid revenue expansion. His background is deliberately capital-markets oriented. Before ACM, McKechnie was Managing Director of Technology Equity Research at Evercore Partners, covering semiconductor and industrial-technology companies; prior to that, Vice President of Investor Relations and Strategic Initiatives at Silver Spring Networks, the smart-grid networking company. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Purdue and an MBA from the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern — a combination that makes him effective at translating ACM's China-centric operations into the vocabulary institutional investors in New York and San Francisco expect. At 60 as of the 2026 proxy, McKechnie was the officer whose signature appeared on all SEC current reports filed in the period reviewed, including the February 26, 2026 Form 8-K announcing fiscal year 2025 results. His total direct equity exposure in the parent company — roughly 208,599 shares in Class A equivalents including exercisable options — is modest relative to the Wang family block, underscoring that economic alignment runs primarily through options rather than outright ownership.

[ACM Research, Inc., DEF 14A (filed April 27, 2026), SEC EDGAR CIK 0001680062](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001680062&type=DEF+14A)

## The Shanghai Subsidiary C-Suite

Because ACM Research's operating substance lives almost entirely inside its subsidiary ACM Research (Shanghai), Inc. — the entity that manufactures SAPS and TEBO tools, generates more than 90 per cent of consolidated revenue, and employs the large majority of ACM's 2,518 full-time-equivalent global workforce as of December 31, 2025 — the Shanghai-side executive appointments carry operational weight that sometimes exceeds what their secondary billing in the NASDAQ parent's filings suggests.

Jian Wang, age 61, has served as Chief Executive Officer and President of ACM Research (Shanghai) since November 2019. He is David Wang's younger brother — a familial relationship that the parent company discloses clearly in its proxy and that represents the most material related-party consideration in ACM's governance architecture. Jian Wang's technical formation differs from his brother's: he holds a Master of Science in Marine Engineering from Kobe University, a Master of Science in Computer Science from Northwestern Polytechnic University, and a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from Southeast University. He joined ACM Shanghai in 2011 as Director of Research and Development, focused on stress-free polishing and electrochemical copper planarization, before advancing to Vice President of R&D and then to the CEO role. As of April 2025, Jian Wang held approximately 150,003 Class B shares, representing a 3.0 per cent interest in that superstructure, and 418,161 Class A equivalents in total.

Lisa Feng, age 67, is Chief Financial Officer of ACM Research (Shanghai). She spent the 2018–2019 period as Chief Accounting Officer and interim CFO of the Fremont parent before transitioning to the subsidiary CFO role when McKechnie was promoted. Her background is corporate accounting: she served as Corporate Controller of Amlogic, the Chinese fabless semiconductor company, from 2008 to 2017 and holds degrees from Southern Connecticut State University and Golden Gate University. The structural importance of her role derives from the fact that ACM Shanghai generates its own financial disclosures as a publicly listed company on the STAR Market, requiring a separate, Chinese-GAAP–compatible finance function independent of the NASDAQ reporting chain that McKechnie manages.

Sotheara Cheav, age 74, was elevated to Senior Vice President, Manufacturing at the NASDAQ parent level in April 2025, having previously held that title at the Shanghai subsidiary since May 2019. He has been with ACM in manufacturing roles since 2011. Fuping Chen, age 44, leads sales into mainland Chinese fabs as Vice President, Sales China at ACM Shanghai, a role he has held since January 2018; before joining ACM he spent four years at SK Hynix. The Chinese sales function Chen directs — selling to SMIC, YMTC, Hua Hong, and CXMT — is the engine of ACM's domestic-substitution revenue.

## The NASDAQ Board: A Compact, Governance-Minded Four

ACM Research's NASDAQ parent operates with one of the smallest boards among companies of comparable revenue scale in the semiconductor equipment sector: four directors, three of them independent, all elected annually, none serving in staggered classes so long as Class B shares retain a voting majority.

**Haiping Dun** (age 77, director since 2003) is the board's most tenured independent member and its Lead Director. A PhD materials scientist from Stanford, Dun built his career at Intel Corporation, where he served as Senior Director from 1983 to 2004 — covering the period during which Intel's materials-engineering standards shaped the global semiconductor supply chain — before moving to Champion Microelectronic Corporation, a Taiwan-based integrated circuit company, where he served as President from 2008 through 2018. Dun chairs the Compensation Committee and sits on Audit; his dual role as Lead Director and Compensation Chair concentrates independent oversight in a single experienced hand.

**Tracy Liu** (age 61, director since September 2016) chairs the Audit Committee and is the board's principal financial expert. She is Managing Partner of H&M International CPAs, LLP and the founder of H&M Financial Consulting, which she operated from 2006 to 2016 providing international tax and accounting work to high-technology companies. A graduate of Nankai University with a master's degree in Accounting and Tax from Golden Gate University, Liu has been the independent voice closest to ACM's external-audit relationship; the company's auditor throughout the STAR Market era has been Ernst & Young Hua Ming LLP, the Chinese-affiliate firm chosen precisely because it can sign off on both the consolidated US GAAP financials and the Shanghai subsidiary's STAR Market disclosures.

**Charles Pappis** (age 65, director since March 2025) joined the board as Pappis replaced Chenming Hu, whose term expired at the June 2025 annual meeting. Pappis spent thirty years at Applied Materials as Vice President and General Manager before founding Pappis Consulting in 2016. He chairs the Nominating and Governance Committee and sits on Audit, adding applied-materials process and manufacturing experience to a board that had tilted toward materials science academia and finance. His Stanford Executive MBA and Worcester Polytechnic undergraduate degree in Materials Science complement the board's existing technical depth.

**Chenming Hu** — the celebrated UC Berkeley professor emeritus and FinFET co-inventor who served the industry as TSMC's Chief Technology Officer from 2001 to 2004 — served as an independent ACM director until June 12, 2025. His presence on the board during the critical 2016–2025 scaling period, while never explicitly instrumental in disclosed decisions, lent the company a degree of semiconductor-industry credibility that mattered during institutional road shows and customer conversations. Pappis's Applied Materials background provides an operational replacement orientation rather than a scientific-prestige one.

## Dual-Class Capital and the Voting Architecture

The governance reality of ACM Research is defined by the dual-class share structure more than any board resolution. Class A common stock carries one vote per share; Class B carries twenty. Wang's family holdings — 4,166,808 Class B shares distributed across himself, family trusts, his son Brian, his daughter Sophia, and related entities — together with his Class A holdings gave him 57.2 per cent of total voting power as of the April 2026 record date, against a total float of roughly 66.2 million share equivalents. BlackRock held 7,420,308 Class A shares (12.1 per cent of Class A, 4.6 per cent of total votes) and Shanghai Pudong Innotek Capital Co., Ltd. held 3,358,728 Class A shares (5.5 per cent of Class A, 2.1 per cent of votes) per the 2026 proxy. The practical effect is that Wang can veto any ordinary or special resolution without the cooperation of a single outside investor.

[ACM Research, Inc., DEF 14A (2026), Beneficial Ownership Table; ACM Research 10-K for FY2025, filed March 2, 2026]

## Dual-Listing Governance: the STAR Market Layer

The November 2021 STAR Market IPO of ACM Shanghai created a second governance layer that operates under Chinese company law, SSE listing rules, and CSRC oversight, simultaneously with the NASDAQ parent's Delaware/SEC framework. ACM Research explicitly described itself in SEC filings as "one of the first publicly traded U.S. companies to complete an initial public offering of shares of a mainland China subsidiary on the STAR Market," a structural novelty that has attracted sustained investor-relations attention. As of December 31, 2025, ACM Research held 74.6 per cent of ACM Shanghai's outstanding shares. Following a February 2026 secondary sale of approximately 4.8 million shares at RMB 160.0 per share (approximately $23.05), that holding declined to 73.7 per cent. The ACM Shanghai private placement completed in September 2025 raised approximately $623 million — proceeds the 10-K notes are "generally not available for distribution to ACM Research" and are ring-fenced for mainland China operations.

ACM Shanghai has its own board of directors and supervisory board under Chinese company law. Jian Wang leads the subsidiary as CEO and President, and Lisa Feng as CFO functions as the primary interface with STAR Market disclosure requirements. The parent-subsidiary structure means that the interests of ACM Shanghai's minority public shareholders — approximately 25 per cent of the subsidiary's float as of the frozen date — can diverge from those of the NASDAQ parent's stockholders, a risk factor the company has disclosed consistently since the STAR IPO. The Conflict of Interest Policy adopted by ACM Research's board in October 2017 requires written notice of related-party transactions above $100,000, reviewed by the audit committee under Item 404 of Regulation S-K. The company disclosed no reportable related-party transactions since January 1, 2025 other than standard compensation arrangements — a clean reading that nonetheless coexists with the structural fact that the subsidiary's principal supplier of robotic delivery system subassemblies, Ninebell Company Limited, is an ACM equity investee.

The interplay of Wang's unassailable voting control at the NASDAQ parent, his brother's management of the Shanghai operating company, and the ring-fenced capital and disclosure requirements of the STAR Market subsidiary constitutes the governance architecture within which all product development, customer contracting, and capital allocation decisions at ACM Research are made. Wang's $632,769 total compensation for fiscal year 2025 — producing a 21-to-1 CEO-to-median-employee ratio on a workforce whose median annual compensation was $30,498, largely in RMB — is a numerical reminder of how much the company's value creation flows through a Fremont founder who retains direct control of the machine he built.

> "2025 was a year of strong execution for ACM. We delivered record annual revenue of $901 million, up 15% year over year, outperforming estimated China WFE. We strengthened our foundation for long-term growth by advancing new products, expanding our global production capacity, and enhancing global funding initiatives."
>
> — Dr. David H. Wang, CEO and President, ACM Research, February 26, 2026

> "We believe ACM has the customers, the products, the capacity and the capital to execute on our global business plan and we remain committed to our long-term target of $4 billion in revenue."
>
> — Dr. David H. Wang, February 26, 2026

[ACM Research, Inc., Form 8-K Exhibit 99.1 (Q4 2025 earnings press release, filed February 26, 2026)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1680062/000162828026011998/acmr-q42025xearningsreleas.htm)
